name: Kingdom of Romania
info: A monarchy under the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen dynasty from 1881 to 1947, which doubled in size after the First World War as Greater Romania and ended with the abdication of King Michael I.

facts.predecessor: Principality of Romania (the united principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia)

t: The Romanian parliament raised the country to a kingdom in 1881, three years after the Treaty of Berlin recognised its independence from the Ottoman Empire.
After the First World War Transylvania, Bessarabia and Bukovina joined the kingdom, and by 1920 Romania was more than twice its 1914 size.
Carol II's royal dictatorship of 1938 gave way in 1940 to the military dictatorship of Ion Antonescu, and the monarchy was abolished on 30 December 1947.
dyk: In 1857, before the kingdom existed, the first oil refinery in the world was built at Ploiești; by the late 1930s Romania was one of the top oil exporters.
ev: Parliament raises Romania to a kingdom and Carol I is crowned king
Romania enters the Second Balkan War against Bulgaria and acquires Southern Dobruja
Romania enters the First World War on the Entente side; the Central Powers occupy Wallachia and Bucharest by the end of the year
Representatives of the Transylvanian Romanians at Alba Iulia proclaim the union of Transylvania with Romania
A land reform redistributes land to the peasants but does little to improve farming
Carol II dismisses the Goga government and institutes a royal dictatorship
After territorial losses Carol II abdicates and Ion Antonescu rules with full powers
King Michael I abdicates and parliament proclaims the Romanian People's Republic

sections.foundation:
The kingdom grew out of the union of Moldavia and Wallachia. In 1859 Alexandru Ioan Cuza became prince of both principalities under the nominal suzerainty of the Ottoman Empire, and in 1862 they were formally united as the Principality of Romania, with Bucharest as its capital. In 1866 a coalition of Conservatives and radical Liberals forced Cuza to abdicate, and the German prince and Prussian officer Karl of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was appointed Prince of Romania to secure Prussian backing for unity and independence. He took the Romanian form of his name, Carol.

Ottoman suzerainty had become a legal fiction: Romania had its own flag and anthem, and from 1867 its own currency. After the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878, known locally as the Romanian War of Independence, the Treaty of Berlin of 1878 recognised Romania's independence and gave it Northern Dobruja, while it had to surrender southern Bessarabia to Russia. In March 1881, as an assertion of full sovereignty, parliament raised the country to a kingdom, and Carol was crowned king.
sections.socioeconomy:
The economy was mainly agricultural. In 1919 about 72% of Romanians worked in farming, and the peasantry was among the poorest in the region, with one of Europe's highest birth rates. The prewar Regat was a land of large estates worked by peasants with little or no land. The land reform of 1921 accomplished little: large landowners still held up to 30% of the land, the new plots were too small to feed their owners, and farming collapsed in the Great Depression.

Industry grew from mills, brick and sugar factories founded before the kingdom; the first oil refinery in the world had been built at Ploiești in 1857, and the CFR railway was founded in 1880. After 1918 the Malaxa company, founded by Nicolae Malaxa in 1921, made Romania self-sufficient in locomotives by 1930, and the Reșița works added heavy industry. In 1938 Romania produced 6.6 million tons of crude oil and was one of the top oil exporters. The 1930 census counted 18,057,028 people, 71.9% of them Romanians. Schools followed the French model, but in practice peasants had almost no chance of an education.
sections.military:
Romania stayed out of the first Balkan war but entered the Second Balkan War in June 1913 against Bulgaria: 330,000 troops crossed the Danube, one army occupying Southern Dobruja and another threatening Sofia. In 1916 it declared war on the Central Powers. Its offensive into Transylvania was quickly crushed, and by the end of 1916 the Central Powers held Wallachia, Dobruja, Bucharest and the oil fields. Despite fierce resistance, notably at the Battle of Mărășești, Russia's withdrawal left Romania surrounded, and it signed the Armistice of Focșani and in May 1918 the Treaty of Bucharest. It returned to the field on 10 November 1918, and in 1919 its troops occupied Budapest and ended Béla Kun's regime.

Wartime industry turned fortification guns into field and anti-aircraft artillery, and the Danube fleet had four river monitors built at Galați. Between the wars the Industria Aeronautică Română built aircraft such as the IAR 80, and factories produced guns, mortars and machine guns under French, Czechoslovak, German and British licences. In the Second World War Romania fought with the Axis until King Michael's Coup of 1944 brought it over to the Allies.
sections.governance:
Romania was a constitutional monarchy ruled by Carol I and his descendants. After King Ferdinand died in 1927, his son Carol was passed over because of earlier marital scandals, and the boy Michael reigned with a regency until Carol returned after three years in exile, with the support of the National Peasants' Party, and proclaimed himself king. Until 1938 governments kept the form, if not always the substance, of liberal constitutional rule. The 1923 constitution let the king dissolve parliament at will, and there were over 25 governments between 1930 and 1940.

The National Liberal Party grew clientelist and nationalist and lost power in 1927 to the National Peasants' Party. Antisemitic and ultra-nationalist parties gained ground, above all the fascist Iron Guard, which practised assassination: it killed Prime Minister Ion Duca in 1933 and Armand Călinescu in 1939. In February 1938 Carol II set up a royal dictatorship under a new constitution, and the Iron Guard leader Corneliu Zelea Codreanu was killed in custody that November. The country was divided into 33 counties, after 1925 into 71, and briefly in 1938 into ten ținuturi under royal residents.
sections.impact:
Squeezed between the Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian and Russian Empires, the kingdom looked to the West, particularly France, for its cultural, educational and administrative models. The term Old Kingdom, or Regat, later distinguished its prewar lands of Wallachia, Moldavia and Dobruja from Greater Romania.

At the end of the First World War assemblies in Transylvania, Bessarabia and Bukovina voted for union with Romania, and the Treaty of Saint-Germain, the Treaty of Trianon and the Treaty of Paris of 1920 assigned most of these lands to it. In 1920 Romania was more than twice its 1914 size. The expansion roused the enmity of Bulgaria, the Soviet Union and especially Hungary. Greater Romania held large minorities, above all Hungarians and Germans, who were effectively shut out of politics by a rule that state employees speak Romanian, though they kept their own schools, publications and courts; these rights were not extended to other minorities, Jews in particular. French influence was strongest in the early 1920s, German influence in the 1930s, and the oil industry drew German and Italian interest.
sections.decline:
The Great Union did not survive the Second World War. The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact of 1939 recorded the Soviet interest in Bessarabia, and in 1940, under pressure from Nazi Germany or the Soviet Union, Romania ceded most of the lands it had gained after 1918, keeping only the southern halves of Bukovina and Transylvania. Carol II, increasingly unpopular, was forced to abdicate and named General Ion Antonescu prime minister with full powers. Under Antonescu's military dictatorship the country was renamed Legionary Romania, and King Michael I was a figurehead.

Romania fought on the side of the Axis until King Michael's Coup against Antonescu in 1944, after which the kingdom became a constitutional monarchy again, changed sides to the Allies and recovered Northern Transylvania. The influence of the Soviet Union and the policies of Communist-dominated coalition governments led to the end of the monarchy: on 30 December 1947 Michael I abdicated, and parliament proclaimed the Romanian People's Republic, a Soviet satellite state.

summary: The Kingdom of Romania was a Hohenzollern monarchy proclaimed in 1881 on the independent union of Moldavia and Wallachia. It gained Transylvania, Bessarabia and Bukovina after the First World War, slid into royal and then military dictatorship, fought for the Axis and then the Allies, and became a people's republic at the end of 1947.
references: Treptow, Kurt W., A History of Romania (1996)
Lampe, John R., Balkan Economic History, 1550–1950: From Imperial Borderlands to Developing Nations (Indiana University Press, 1982)
Goleșteanu-Jacobs, Raluca, Habsburg Galicia and the Romanian Kingdom: Sociocultural Development, 1866–1914 (Routledge, 2023)

pointDescs.1881: Parliament raises the independent principality to a kingdom and Carol I is crowned.
pointDescs.1907: The first of four river monitors built at Galați, Lascăr Catargiu, is launched.
pointDescs.1913: Romania joins the Second Balkan War against Bulgaria and acquires Southern Dobruja.
pointDescs.1916: Romania enters the First World War; the Central Powers take Wallachia, Dobruja and Bucharest.
pointDescs.1918: Bessarabia and Transylvania proclaim union with Romania as the war ends.
pointDescs.1920: The Treaty of Trianon confirms the new lands, and Romania is more than twice its 1914 size.
pointDescs.1929: The Great Depression destabilises the country; the government represses the miners' strike in Valea Jiului.
pointDescs.1933: Prime Minister Ion Duca dissolves the Iron Guard and is assassinated by its legionnaires.
pointDescs.1938: Romania produces 6.6 million tons of crude oil, and Carol II institutes a royal dictatorship.
pointDescs.1940: Romania cedes most of its post-1918 lands, and Carol II abdicates in favour of Ion Antonescu's rule.
pointDescs.1944: King Michael's Coup removes Antonescu and Romania changes sides to the Allies.
pointDescs.1947: Michael I abdicates and the Romanian People's Republic is proclaimed.

notes: The article's World War II and post-war sections are empty; those years rest on its lead and the end of the interwar section only.
The lead dates the crowning to 25 March [O.S. 13 March] 1881, the history section to parliament's vote on 15 March and the crowning on 10 May; only the year 1881 is given.
The article does not say what the 1947 Soviet pressure involved beyond 'influence'; left general. The 1930 return of Carol II is dated from 'three years in exile' after 1927.
